title: The park swing confrontation and his name Bubber
summary: Barred from the chain swings, he refuses to leave one; he explains his boyhood name Bubber Sublette and escapes a gang of boys.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Then I wanted to go to a park in Indianapolis where they have lawn swings and they have chain swings, but they didn't allow colored people to walk children to swing on the swings, chain swings, you know. But you could swing on the lawn swings, you know, old lawn swings with backs to them that four people could sit in. Well, I thought I'd tell my mother to let me go to the park. She says, you can go to the park but you get back by the time I get from

the store. I said, okay.
So as I boy I never knew my name was going
to be JB.

That was your middle name --
and your last name?

Sublette. But the boy that
they took with me to the park, his name was JB. He
was younger than me and we go get in the swings, the
chain swings. But I wasn't thinking of creating
nothing, just get in the swing. I don't know what
possessed me or plodded me to get in the swing, but
I got in the swing and I'm swinging and I want to go
over, you know. I want to go over. So he's there
swinging, swinging and I was swinging and oh, I stand
up in time to get off. So a couple of kids come over
and say, 'Get out of that swing.' Nobody answered him
then. So a little while later about four or five more
kids come when the other kids were there. 'Okay, get

out of the swing." So the boy, JB, got out of the swing but I stayed in the swing and about four or five more boys came over. Must have been about fifty boys around the swing to tell me to get out of the swing. I look over here on the one side, there was a park guard and a matron. I looked over on the other side there's two or three colored people over there so they can see what's happening.

So they hollered again, "Get out of that swing." I said, "When the cat dies," which means when the swing gets down to where it dies of its own momentum I would get out. So I let the swing calm down, calm down, calm down, calm down, and it finally gets down to where I can step out when the swing is not swinging. As soon as I stepped on the ground the boys attacked me. Get the point? When they attacked me, I'd been seeing so many pictures in life that I knew more about how to get out of a gang than they did, you know. So I ducked the guy that hit at me this way, the one guy kicked at me, I went in the crowd, got under the legs and came out right behind them, you know. And I run from there over to a push

merry-go-round and I got over there and the park guard and the matron never said a word, so I figured I would -- I was now mad because they wouldn't say nothing and the guys could do what they wanted to do and there was about fifty of them over there by the tree. So I thought I would wait to see what happened about this happening, and the tears started rolling down my cheeks and I had deck overalls on, the pants, and down the side of the pants I had a knife that I play mumble-peg with, you know. So I get this knife out of the side and I opened up the knife, and while they were laughing and celebrating at what they had just done, and I go to this crowd of boys, and I ain't thinking about nothing but going to this crowd of boys -- first come, first served.
